newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - Enron's $440 million gas dispute.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Enron's $440 million gas dispute.

text.p: Enron Corp. paid $440 million to settle a long-running dispute over a British natural gas supply contract with Phillips Petroleum Co., Britain's BG Plc and Italian oil consortium Agip SpA, the companies said on Monday.

Enron, one of the world's largest natural gas and electricity companies, said it will post an after-tax charge of $450 million, or $1.80 per share, tied to the settlement, resulting in a loss for the second quarter.

Although the settlement lifted a cloud of uncertainty hanging over Enron's stock, the company also signalled that hedging losses and costs of building a domestic electric retail operation would contribute to the second-quarter loss, analysts said.
"Places where they anticipated selling gas and electricity just didn't work out," said Howard Weil Labouisse & Friedrichs analyst Susan Weaver.

Under the contract, an Enron subsidiary had agreed to buy British North Sea gas from the producers under the "take or pay" contract. In September 1995, however, Enron balked after a delay in the construction of two power plants to be fueled by the gas and prevailing North Sea gas prices fell far below the contract prices.

Under the settlement, the take-or pay contract was amended to a firm 15-year supply contract and terms reduced to reflect the lower North Sea gas prices. The total volume of gas to be lifted from the offshore Judy and Joanne project, better known as the J-Block, will remain essentially the same, the companies said.

"A significant amount of the gas has already been marketed longer term," Enron Chairman Ken Lay said. "The important thing is, we believe what we agreed to here gets the price of this gas down to a level where we can be competitive in the U.K. market going forward."

Phillips, which owns a 36.5 percent interest in J-Block and operates the field, will receive $160 million under the settlement. BG Exploration & Production Ltd. owns 30.5 percent and will receive $134.2 million. Agip owns 33 percent.

Phillips in April began reinjecting associated gas back into the formation so that it could produce oil from the field. The move eased the financial pressure on the producers and was seen as pressing Enron to agree to a settlement.

The J-Block produces about 40,000 barrels of oil per day. As a result of the settlement, output in July is expected to jump to an average 260 million cubic feet a day of gas and 95,000 barrels a day of liquids, Phillips said.

Enron's decision not to take gas deliveries under the initial contract also sparked litigation over its transmission agreement with owners of the Central Area Transmission System. The system owners are Amoco UK Exploration Ltd., British Gas North Sea Holdings, British Gas Exploration & Production, Amerada Hess Ltd., Phillips Petroleum United Kingdom Ltd., Fina Exploration Co. and Agip (UK) Ltd.
A decision in that case is expected from the High Court in London on June 3, but will not affect Enron's settlement with the producers, the companies said.
Enron said it expects to report a primary loss per share in the range of $1.40 to $1.45. The Houston-based company earned $222 million, or 88 cents per share, in the quarter ended March 31.
Enron's stock fell 25 cents to $40.50, and Phillips rose 37.5 cents to $42.875 on the New York Stock Exchange in late trading.
